description: Who owns a field's value universe decides what an unrecognised value MEANS. Where the ENGINE owns it — fql_kind, because a language plugin maps its grammar onto the kind vocabulary rather than extending it, and role on FIND usages, minted by the read pass — no corpus can hold a value outside the list, so naming one is a fact about the query and is refused naming what is accepted. Where the CORPUS owns it, an unstored value stays a fast, honest empty answer. Both halves are pinned here, because the boundary is as load-bearing as the rule: the commit that made fql_kind = 'impl' an error had to leave guard_kind = 'ifdef' answering nothing. Every case says which side of the line it stands on.

cases.name: control_a_known_kind_filters_the_outline
cases.description: Anchors the unknown-kind case below: a kind inside the universe filters the same file's outline to its one struct, so the refusal below is about the value and not about the verb.

cases.name: an_unknown_kind_value_is_refused_not_silently_empty
cases.description: 'impl' reads like a kind and is not one — Rust's impl_item maps to 'class'. The outline used to answer header-only silence, indistinguishable from 'this file has none of those'. It is now refused, and the refusal hands back the whole accepted universe rather than only saying no.

cases.name: an_unknown_kind_is_refused_under_its_alias_too
cases.description: 'kind' is the DSL alias for fql_kind. Membership is tested against the canonical field, so the alias cannot slip past — and the message quotes back the spelling the agent typed, or it reads as being about a field they did not write.

cases.name: the_negation_is_refused_as_well_as_the_equality
cases.description: != 'impl' is the more dangerous direction: it excludes nothing and returns everything, so the wrong answer looks like a legitimate one rather than a suspicious zero.

cases.name: a_pattern_on_an_engine_owned_field_is_not_a_value
cases.description: The refusal reads = and != only. A pattern names no value: LIKE '%_block' is a legitimate question about the block kinds, and a regex matching none of them would be a legitimate question with an empty answer. Refusing patterns would have closed a query shape the engine answers well.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind LIKE '%_block' LIMIT 3

cases.name: the_rendered_spelling_of_the_kindless_row_is_inside_the_universe
cases.description: A row nothing maps stores the empty kind, and SHOW outline renders it as 'unknown' — all three emit paths do, the columnar outline twice and the in-memory one once. Filtering on what the engine just printed answered these three rows before this check existed, so a universe that knew only the stored spelling would have refused a query the engine's own output invites — the engine contradicting a value it had printed. Both spellings are accepted; the rendering decides which one an agent sees. This case is the regression guard: it fails the moment the refusal knows one spelling and the renderer another.
cases.fql: SHOW outline OF 'crates/forgeql-core/src/ast/enrich/casts.rs' ALL WHERE fql_kind = 'unknown'

cases.name: control_a_known_role_answers_on_find_usages
cases.description: Anchors the role case below, and pins that role is the second engine-owned universe rather than fql_kind with a special case. code is the resolved-identifier role, and the eighteen such sites sit in three files — which is why LIMIT 3 returns all eighteen rows rather than three: on FIND usages the limit counts FILES and every site of a selected file is returned. Those eighteen are what the refusal below must leave undisturbed.
cases.fql: FIND usages OF 'ClauseTarget' WHERE role = 'code' LIMIT 3

cases.name: the_rendered_empty_role_is_inside_the_universe
cases.description: A site with no role at all renders as the empty string — the in-memory backend tags none of them, and the CSV renderer prints that. It is a value an agent can read off an answer, so it must be a value they can filter on: a universe that refuses what the engine printed contradicts itself, the same lesson the outline's 'unknown' spelling taught. What this case pins is the ACCEPTANCE — that the value is not refused — and nothing more. It does NOT prove the filter can reach it: a field a row does not carry fails every equality arm, the empty string included, so role = '' matches nothing on either backend. On this indexed corpus the zero is right anyway, since the columnar read pass tags every site it finds; on the in-memory backend, where the empty spelling is the one actually printed, it is the same false zero the kindless kinds have, and it is pinned with them in open_defects.
cases.fql: FIND usages OF 'ClauseTarget' WHERE role = '' LIMIT 3

cases.name: an_unknown_role_is_refused_on_find_usages
cases.description: The occurrence roles are minted by the read pass that finds the site, so they are engine-owned on the same terms as the kinds. 'banana' used to answer a silent zero, which on a blast-radius query reads as 'nothing references this that way'.
cases.fql: FIND usages OF 'ClauseTarget' WHERE role = 'banana' LIMIT 3

cases.name: control_a_corpus_owned_value_answers_empty_and_is_not_refused
cases.description: The boundary of the whole change, and it is as load-bearing as the rule. guard_kind takes its values from what the enrichers found in the code — this corpus stores 'attribute' and 'preprocessor' — so 'ifdef' is a value the corpus does not hold rather than one the engine cannot mint. Its empty answer is a fact about the code and must stay an answer. A refusal here would mean the check had leaked past the two fields that own their values.

cases.name: control_a_known_kind_answers_on_find
cases.description: Anchors the case below on the FIND verb at corpus scale: a kind inside the universe answers rows on zephyr.

cases.name: an_unknown_kind_is_refused_on_find_too
cases.description: The outline case pins one verb; the defect was on every filtering verb. FIND at least printed a zero total, but zero is still a claim about the corpus where an error is the fact about the query. The check runs once per operation over the op's clauses, ahead of dispatch, so it reaches every verb that carries a clause and both storage backends — this case is what proves it did not land in one verb.
